title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Ypsilanti hits pause on power upgrades tied to a big U-M computing project.

lines.text: Good evening and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're digging into a fresh pause in Washtenaw County that could ripple across how the state handles big power demands from these facilities.
That sounds like the Ypsilanti Township story, right?
Exactly. On Tuesday the township board approved a 180-day moratorium on new or expanded high-voltage utility facilities.
Why now? What's driving this specific freeze?
It's tied directly to a proposed University of Michigan research computing center backed by Los Alamos National Laboratory.
So this isn't just any data center — it's a university-linked project with national lab ties.
Right. The board wants time to study the impacts before any major electrical infrastructure moves forward.
What kind of impacts are they worried about? Power strain, I assume.
Power is the big one, but also how it affects the grid that's already seeing growth from AI needs.
And residents nearby — how are they reacting so far?
The summary points to concerns over power and water demands that could ultimately hit taxpayers for upgrades.
That connects to the bigger picture we've seen in other townships this week.
It does. This feels like part of a pattern where local leaders are hitting the brakes to get ahead of projects.
Let's talk about the history here. How long has this tension been building in Washtenaw?
From what we've tracked, county officials have been pitching these as economic wins with jobs and tax revenue, but residents keep raising the power and water questions.
So the pitch is jobs and revenue, the pushback is infrastructure costs.
Exactly. The moratorium gives the township board time to weigh those trade-offs before anything gets locked in.
What happens next? Does this delay the U-M project itself or just the power lines?
It specifically pauses new or expanded high-voltage facilities, so the computing center's electrical needs are on hold for study.
And if the study finds big issues, could it reshape or block the project?
That's the intent — to have concrete data before approvals move forward.
This seems to echo what we're seeing in other places like Garfield and Solon townships.
It does. Let's move into some of those quick hits from the past couple days.
Starting with Solon Township — they extended their data center freeze another six months yesterday.
Yes, leaders recommended keeping the moratorium through early next year while they update zoning rules.
What are the main resident concerns driving that?
Noise, traffic, and utility costs — and nearby West Michigan communities are watching closely.
Similar story in another West Michigan town that also pushed its ban out to early 2027.
That extension gives residents more time to examine power demand, noise, and water use before any large projects advance.
Gaines Township is taking a different approach with sound studies.
Officials there will measure decibel levels at a proposed site to see how much residents would hear from cooling fans and generators.
If it exceeds limits, that could block or reshape the project entirely.
Homeowners within a few miles now have a way to get concrete data on daily life impacts.
Up north, township leaders endorsed state bills to make data centers pay more for grid upgrades.
The idea is that could lower electric bills for residents, but only if local governments keep leverage over projects.
That signals growing pushback against unlimited growth.
Garfield Township voted on Wednesday to halt new proposals for a full year while they research power, water, and noise limits.
That pause prevents developers from filing before new rules are in place.
Lowell Township is still working on its own ordinance after months of debate.
The rules will set where facilities can go and what limits apply to power and noise in Kent County.
A new state bill would require data centers to disclose water use, which addresses aquifer and supply concerns.
Communities want that data before projects get approved.
Lawmakers in Lansing are also reviewing bills on tax breaks and power rules that could speed up or slow down projects needing hundreds of megawatts.
Residents might see higher bills or new local revenue depending on what passes.
And back in Washtenaw, leaders are highlighting jobs and taxes from the new proposal even as residents question the demands.
The project would add significant load to a grid already strained by AI growth.
Taxpayers within driving distance would ultimately pay for any needed upgrades.
So the Ypsilanti pause feels like a direct response to those same pressures.
It does — giving the township breathing room on the electrical side of things.
What kind of history are we seeing with these moratoriums across the state?
Several townships have used them to update zoning and gather resident input on noise, traffic, and costs before anything moves forward.
And the stakes for electric bills are real if upgrades get passed along.
Water draw and farmland protection come up a lot too in the debates.
Towns are trying to balance potential tax revenue against those long-term infrastructure hits.
The pattern suggests more communities will keep pausing until they have clearer rules.
What happens next on the state level with those bills on power costs and water reporting?
They'll need to move through the legislature, and local leverage seems key to whether residents see any relief on bills.
For now the local pauses are buying time.
Let's check what's on deck for listeners who want to follow along.
The tracker shows no major public meetings listed for tonight or tomorrow in the immediate areas we've discussed.
Folks can keep an eye on township websites for any updates on zoning reviews or public comment periods.
That covers the landscape for now.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Ypsilanti Township Freezes Power Lines Over University Data Center Plan
